chawasi.place: Kothi Mahog, Chawasi area, Karsog, Mandi district
chawasi.summary: Nag Chawasi Siddh is the presiding deity ('gadhpati') of the Chawasi area of Karsog valley, seated at Mahog, ruling over roughly 16 panchayats including six other devi-devta temples. 2026 was unusually eventful, with several first-ever or century-plus-gap appearances at fairs outside his own area.
legend: Locals believe that a king of the former Suket princely state once gifted Nag Chawasi Siddh a large cauldron (kadhai), still kept in the temple and used to hold the deity's ceremonial tongs.

fairs.name: Nalwar Mela, Karsog (first-ever attendance)
fairs.when: District-level fair usually 5-11 April
fairs.what_happens: Formal procession (shahi jalab) into Karsog, ceremonial meeting of chariots, overnight halts at the Mamleshwar temple and the Laxmi Narayan temple, Purana Bazaar.

fairs.name: Suket Devta Mela, Sundernagar
fairs.when: State-level fair, usually mid-to-late March
fairs.what_happens: Multi-day walking procession, halt at Purana Bazaar on the first night, formal welcome by Sundernagar residents, chariot competitions.

fairs.name: Rowa Mela, Himrigarh (historic meeting)
fairs.when: Late September
fairs.what_happens: First-ever meeting (mahamilan) with Gadhpati Shri Kui Kanda Nag of Tandi (Aani, Kullu), Nag Gadumi, and Mata Shani Durga.

fairs.name: Sareulsar yatra (to meet mother Budhi Nagin)
fairs.when: Around Ashadh Sankranti
fairs.what_happens: Pilgrimage to meet the deity's mother, Budhi Nagin; 2025 also saw a first-ever meeting with brother-deity Chotru Nag.

rituals_customs: An annual 'Green Chawasi Siddh' campaign has women's groups (mahila mandals) plant trees on the deity's Prakatya Diwas (manifestation day).
The Mahog temple's foundation was laid in 2017, finished in 2025; Pran Pratishtha Maha Puj held 28 May-5 June 2025 with visiting deities from Suket, Magru, Mangarh, Raghupurgarh and Janjagarh.
visiting: Main temple is at Kothi Mahog in the Chawasi area of Karsog subdivision.

chindi.place: Chindi village, about 13-14 km from Karsog town on the Karsog-Shimla road, Mandi district, Himachal Pradesh, at roughly 1,400-1,825 m altitude
chindi.summary: Chindi Mata temple, in Chindi village of the Karsog valley, is dedicated to Durga in her fierce Chandi (Chandika) form and is best known for the legend that its layout was mapped out by a colony of ants. The temple has an ancient eight-armed (ashtabhuji) stone idol and is built with fine traditional Himachali wood carving. It is one of the valley's main shakti shrines, drawing pilgrims from as far as Delhi, Kolkata and Mumbai, especially for its August fair.
legend: According to local legend, the goddess appeared to a priest in a dream as a young unmarried girl (kanya) and showed him, through a trail marked out by a colony of ants, the exact plan for the temple, and even for its adjoining pond and storeroom.
Locals say the temple's name 'Chindi' comes from 'chinti' (ant), because the site's layout was traced by the ants rather than by any human hand.
Chindi Mata is regarded locally as a kumari (unmarried) goddess who dedicated her life entirely to protecting dharma and her devotees rather than marrying.

One version of her journey story says she first set out from a place called Jufar, was welcomed as a sister by Dev Mahasu at the village of Shiva, then was so loved by the people of Bajo that she called that village her maternal home (maika), and finally settled permanently at Chindi after being captivated by its beauty.
Devotees believe childless couples who pray sincerely at this temple can be blessed with children.

fairs.name: Chindi Mata Mela (Chakranth)
fairs.when: A fixed three-day fair, 2-4 August every year, held at the Chakranth mela ground near the temple
fairs.what_happens: The fair opens on 2 August with a grand procession of the goddess's chariot, ceremonial umbrella (chhatra) and band, escorted by the temple's kardars (officials), from the temple to the Chakranth mela ground. It closes on the evening of 4 August with a ceremonial farewell of the goddess. In 2025 the organisers held the mela without any DJ music or cultural-evening programme.

rituals_customs: The temple keeps a bhandar (storeroom) where the goddess's costly garments and ornaments are stored, its layout also credited to the ants in legend.
During Navratri, the temple holds special puja, havan and kirtan along with a large community bhandara (free community meal).
The three-day annual fair begins and ends with a formal chariot procession between the temple and the mela ground rather than the goddess simply remaining at the temple.
visiting: The temple is about 13-14 km from Karsog town on the road towards Shimla, roughly 90-100 km from Shimla itself.
It sits among apple orchards and deodar forest at around 1,400-1,825 m altitude.
It is known for its traditional wood-carved architecture in Himachali pagoda style.

dawahad.place: Karsog valley (deity tours the wider Karsog area)
dawahad.summary: Dev Dawahadi is described as the presiding deity ('aaradhya') of Karsog valley, known for periodically touring the region and staying as a guest in local homes. He shares an unusual chariot arrangement with Mamleshwar Mahadev.
rituals_customs: Dev Dawahadi periodically undertakes a village-to-village tour of Karsog valley, staying as a guest in homes across the area as a form of blessing.

A devotee describes a rath (chariot) in which Dev Dawahadi's idol rides seated behind Mamleshwar Mahadev's, a pairing said to be possibly unique in Himachal Pradesh; a related chariot also carries 'Dev Ledhi ji'.
Historically, Dev Dawahadi (along with Nag Belu and Nag Dhamuni) was among the deities who used to attend the Nalwar Mela in Karsog.

dhamuni.summary: Nag Dhamuni is described locally as 'king of four forts', with a domain covering more than half of the Karsog valley. His main temple is at Seri Bungalow, and he is closely tied to the Kunho village fairground and to the Ashadh/Thirshu fair season each June.
legend: Locals believe Nag Dhamuni originally belonged to Dev Chhamahu (Chamahu) of Kullu district, and that he left Dhaman (in Kullu) upset, accompanied by an old woman, travelling toward the Suket (present Karsog) side before finally settling at the Dhamun-Seri Banglo area, which became his karambhoomi (adopted homeland).

Locals tell of a hill-lowering contest between Shri Mool Mahunag and Nag Dhamuni: angered by Dhamuni's trickery, Mahunag used his mace (gurj) to raise the hill back up, and since then the two deities have never met in person.

fairs.name: Mela Seri Bhanju (Nag Panchami pragatotsav)
fairs.when: Starts on Rishi Panchami, a 3-day block-level fair at Seri Bungalow
fairs.what_happens: Celebrated as the deity's 'pragatotsav' (manifestation day); religious rituals, cultural evenings and market stalls over three days.

fairs.name: Ashadh Mela / Thirshu Mela, Jachh-Chauridhar
fairs.when: Starts on Ashadh Sankranti, roughly 16-18 June
fairs.what_happens: Three-day fair; also the occasion each year (on 'Saza Ashadh') when Dev Tebni Mahadev crosses the river to Kotgarhi and Nag Dhamuni comes to Nanj so the two chariots can meet, after which they turn to sit back-to-back — a custom locals describe as carrying a deeper meaning.

fairs.name: Kunho (Kunnu) Mela
fairs.when: 3-day fair, usually 7-9 August
fairs.what_happens: Maa Kamaksha, Nag Pundri and Nag Dhamuni Kunho are welcomed with a shobha yatra by local women's groups at an open fairground about 10 km from Karsog that also has a helipad.

rituals_customs: Historically, Nag Dhamuni was among the deities who used to attend the Nalwar Mela in Karsog, alongside Dev Dawahadi and Nag Belu.
visiting: Main temple at Seri Bungalow (Seri Banglo), Karsog; an old temple photo is occasionally shared showing the earlier structure.

edhneshwar.summary: Edhneshwar Mahadev's temple at Syanj Bagra hosts the annual Thirshu Mela, a multi-day fair known for its cultural evenings with well-known regional folk singers.

fairs.name: Thirshu Mela, Edhneshwar Mahadev
fairs.when: Held around late April/springtime as part of the wider Thirshu fair season
fairs.what_happens: A cultural evening (sanskritik sandhya) featuring well-known regional folk (naati) singers.

visiting: Temple at Syanj Bagra, Karsog.

kajauni.summary: Nag Kajauni is seated at Mamel, close to the Mamleshwar Mahadev temple, and regularly appears alongside Mamleshwar and other Karsog deities at joint fairs and processions.

fairs.name: Nalwar Mela, Karsog
fairs.when: District-level fair, usually 5-11 April
fairs.what_happens: Joint procession and meeting (mahamilan) of chariots on the fair's opening day.

rituals_customs: Nag Kajauni's chariot is regularly seen alongside Maa Kamaksha and Nag Pundri at the Kao Lahaul Mela.
Historically noted alongside Mamleshwar Mahadev, Nag Dhamuni and Nag Sayanj Bagda at a 'devon ka alaukik milan' (divine gathering) at Bhandarnu.
visiting: Temple at Mamel, Karsog, near the Mamleshwar Mahadev temple.

kamaksha.place: Kao village, about 7-8 km from Karsog town, Mandi district, Himachal Pradesh
kamaksha.summary: Maa Kamaksha temple in Kao village is one of the main shakti (goddess) shrines of the Karsog valley, dedicated to Durga in her Kamaksha form. It is built in the traditional wood-and-stone pagoda style typical of the valley and is closely linked to legends of Parashurama and to the old Suket princely state, whose royal family is said to have worshipped Kamaksha as their family deity. Local posts sometimes describe it as one of only a few Kamaksha/Kamakhya temples in the region, alongside the well-known one in Guwahati, Assam (this is a local claim, not something the posts prove).
legend: According to one local tradition, Parashurama did penance at this spot after killing his mother Renuka, and a pleased Maa Kamaksha appeared to him; he then installed her image and founded the temple here.
Another local tradition says the goddess's ashtadhatu (eight-metal) idol was brought from a place called 'Kaoru', which is why the village is named Kao.
Locals believe the goddess slew the demon Mahishasura at this site, so she is worshipped here as Mahishasuramardini.

The temple is said to have served as the rajdevi (royal deity) of the former Suket princely state, and is also described locally as a kuldevi (family deity) shared by the Suket, Bushahr and Kullu ruling families.
Devotees believe a bed kept in a small room beside the main idol is used by the goddess at night; the priest makes the bed fresh each morning and it is said to be found creased, as if slept in.

fairs.name: Ashtami Mela, Kao
fairs.when: Held during Sharadiya (autumn) Navratri, centred on the midnight of Ashtami
fairs.what_happens: Devotees gather at the temple through Navratri; on the night of Ashtami the goddess is believed to give darshan through a local person (possession) at midnight, and devotees seek her blessing for their wishes.

fairs.name: Barshail Mela, Lalag
fairs.when: 2-3 June, fixed
fairs.what_happens: Maa Kamaksha and Nag Pundri ji are seated in their chariots and taken to Lalag village for the fair.

fairs.name: Kunho (Kunnu) Mela
fairs.when: 7-9 August, fixed, three days
fairs.what_happens: Maa Kamaksha, Nag Pundri and Nag Dhamuni Kunho are brought in procession to Kunho/Kunnu village; women's groups (mahila mandals) welcome the chariots with aarti and flowers. In 2025 the goddess's chariot did not appear at the fair, which locals found unusual and worrying for the tradition.

fairs.name: Lahaul Mela
fairs.when: 18 April, fixed; symbolises the wedding of Shiva and Parvati
fairs.what_happens: Mamleshwar Mahadev's chariot and Maa Kamaksha's chariot are brought together in a ceremonial meeting, with bhajans and worship.

fairs.name: Suket Devta Mela, Sundernagar (Kamaksha's occasional attendance)
fairs.when: Same dates as the wider Suket Devta Mela (see [[suket_devta_mela]]); Kamaksha does not attend every year
fairs.what_happens: When she attends, Devi Kamaksha's chariot travels to Sundernagar together with Nag Pundri Kaksh ji.

rituals_customs: A bed is made fresh every morning in a small room beside the main idol, in the belief that the goddess rests there at night.
The temple keeps a very large old dhol (drum), which local tradition associates with Bhima of the Mahabharata.
On Ashtami night during Navratri, the goddess is believed to give darshan through a local devotee who becomes possessed.
visiting: The temple is about 7-8 km from Karsog town.
It is built in traditional wood-carved pagoda style typical of Karsog valley temples.
Navratri (both Chaitra and Sharadiya) is the busiest time for worship and special puja.

kamrunag.place: Kamraah village area, high in the forested hills on the Mandi/Karsog side (Janjehli valley), Mandi district, Himachal Pradesh, at about 3,334 m (10,938 ft)
kamrunag.summary: Kamrunag (also called Bada Dev, 'the great god') is worshipped across the wider Mandi district, including the Karsog valley, as the god of rain, and no rain-dependent activity or major mela in the district is traditionally begun without his blessing. His temple sits beside a small sacred lake deep in deodar forest, where devotees immerse gold, silver and coin offerings as a mark of faith. He is closely linked to several Karsog-area fairs and deities such as Bala Tikka ji and Shikari Mata.
legend: Locals identify Kamrunag with Veer Barbarik (also called Khatu Shyam ji/Babrubhan ji) of the Mahabharata, said to have been one of the most powerful warriors on earth and eager to join the great war.
According to tradition, no rain or snow falls in the region without Kamrunag's will, so devotees and even district officials have historically sought his blessing in times of drought.
Mandi's own International Shivratri Mela is said locally not to begin until Kamrunag has given his consent, and the deity is ceremonially received by Mandi town before the Shivratri mela opens.

fairs.name: Sarahanuli Mela
fairs.when: Held at the main Kamrunag temple; a fixed annual fair (mid-June in local usage, distinct from the 14 June date given in an older general description)
fairs.what_happens: Devotees gather at the temple; other local deities such as Kaula Vir ji also travel to take part.

fairs.name: Maharan (Gohar) Mela
fairs.when: Held twice a year; exact dates vary and are announced each time
fairs.what_happens: Kamrunag ji is said to come to give darshan to his devotees twice a year at this fair; other local deities also attend and give darshan.

fairs.name: Rohanda Mela
fairs.when: 20 Ashadh (Hindu calendar), around early July
fairs.what_happens: Considered the second-biggest mela of the Mangarh area after the Kumraah mela; graced by Dev Bala Tikka ji (Khil Mangarh, Suket) and Dev Kamrunag ji (Mangarh), with Bala Tikka ji traditionally welcoming his father Kamrunag. A larger version, the Chatarwada Jatar, is held once every four years.

fairs.name: Suket Devta Mela, Sundernagar (Kamrunag's attendance)
fairs.when: Same dates as the wider mela (see [[suket_devta_mela]])
fairs.what_happens: Bada Dev Kamrunag ji's chariot travels to Sundernagar along with other Suket-area deities.

rituals_customs: Devotees immerse gold, silver ornaments, coins and cash into the small lake beside the temple as offerings to the deity, a practice followed for generations.
The temple priest acts as a medium (gur) through whom the deity is believed to speak and act.

Devotees and organisers have repeatedly asked, in posts, that visitors keep the temple's surroundings quiet and not disturb it with loud bhajans, dholak or DJ music, out of respect for the deity's preference for a calm environment.
visiting: The temple and lake sit at high altitude (about 3,334 m) inside dense deodar forest, reached via the Janjehli valley side of the Karsog/Mandi hills.

laxmi_narayan.summary: The Laxmi Narayan temple in Karsog's Purana Bazaar is a working neighbourhood temple that hosts a daily evening aarti and also serves as an overnight halting point for visiting deities passing through Karsog town during major fairs.

fairs.name: Janmashtami and Nand Utsav
fairs.when: August-September, on the Hindu calendar dates for Janmashtami and the following Nand Utsav
fairs.what_happens: Temple celebrations marking Krishna's birth and the following Nand Utsav festivities.

rituals_customs: A daily evening aarti (sandhyakaleen aarti) is held at the temple, including for the Narsingh Bhagwan idol housed within the complex.
During the 2026 Nalwar Mela, the visiting deity Gadhpati Shri Nag Chawasi Siddh halted overnight at this temple after taking his evening meal at the Mamleshwar Mahadev temple, Mamel.
visiting: Located in Purana Bazaar, the old market area of Karsog town.

mahasu.place: Bakhras village, Karsog area, Mandi district
mahasu.summary: Dev Mahasu of Bakhras is regarded locally as an avatar of Shiva and a god of justice, distinct from (though sharing a name and origin story with) the well-known four-brother Mahasu tradition of Hanol in Uttarakhand. He attends the annual Suket Devta Mela at Sundernagar from his seat at Bakhras Kothi.
legend: Locals believe Dev Mahasu is an avatar of Lord Shiva who appeared to establish dharma, destroy injustice and protect devotees, and that he delivers swift and true justice, which is why people bring disputes to his court.
Locals believe Mahasu takes four brother forms: Bashik Mahasu, Pabasi Mahasu, Chalda Mahasu and Sangla Mahasu, worshipped with varying local traditions across Himachal.

Locals believe that when Chindi Mata journeyed from Jufar, she first arrived and stayed at 'Shiva' (Shiva village), the seat of Dev Mahasu, who welcomed her and accepted her as his sister before she continued on to Bajo and eventually Chindi.

fairs.name: Suket Devta Mela, Sundernagar (Dev Mahasu's visit)
fairs.when: Deity departs from Bakhras Kothi in March
fairs.what_happens: Deity travels with full retinue to the state-level Suket Devta Mela at Sundernagar; local tradition holds that the plough does not move in the Bakhras area until the deity returns.

rituals_customs: A newly built palanquin (palki) for Dev Mahasu, crafted by a local artisan, was presented at Bisoi village, Khat Bahlad, in 2026.
visiting: Main seat at Bakhras Kothi, Karsog area.

mahunag.place: Bakhari Kothi, near Karsog, Mandi district, Himachal Pradesh
mahunag.summary: Shri Mool Mahunag is the principal Naga deity of the Karsog valley, worshipped at Bakhari Kothi about 25 km from Karsog town. Locals identify him with Karna, the great warrior and giver of charity (Danveer Karna) from the Mahabharata. The temple is one of the most prominent deity seats in the wider Suket-Mandi region and hosts a large annual district-level fair as well as an old, close ritual relationship with the former royal family of Suket.
legend: Locals believe Mahunag is a divine form (avatar) of Karna, the Mahabharata's great warrior known for his charity and fatal vow of friendship to Duryodhana.

Tradition holds that after the war Arjuna, remorseful over killing Karna by deceit, had his body cremated near Tattapani on the Sutlej with the help of naga friends; a naga is said to have emerged from that pyre and settled here, worshipped as Mahunag.

Local legend says Mahunag originated at Shendal in the former Suket state and protected the Suket king from captivity (accounts vary between Mughal and British) by his shakti; grateful, the king built a close ritual bond with the deity, later reflected in the Suket Devta Mela tradition.
Devotees believe Mahunag's blessing wards off ailments, enemies and misfortune, and that wronging his devotees brings karmic consequences.
Gold donations are traditionally avoided in Mahunag worship because his idol is silver, not gold.
A snake-bite victim's ritual 'baandh' (binding) is offered to the Naga, who is regarded as lord over poison.

fairs.name: District-level Shri Mool Mahunag Mela
fairs.name_hi: जिला स्तरीय श्री मूल माहूंनाग मेला
fairs.when: Usually starts around Jyeshtha Sankranti, roughly 14-15 May, and runs about 5 days
fairs.what_happens: A multi-day fair with a formal shobha yatra of the deity to the fair ground, cultural nights, folk music/dance, a bhandara, and a closing ceremony.

fairs.name: Suket Devta Mela, Sundernagar (Mahunag's visit)
fairs.when: Departs Bakhari Kothi for this state-level fair in March, walking roughly 120 km; return timing varies by year
fairs.what_happens: Mahunag travels on foot with his rath to Sundernagar for the state-level Suket Devta Mela, a tradition since 1902 honouring the historic link between Mahunag and the Suket royal family, returning afterward to Bakhari Kothi.

fairs.name: Rath Yatra (chariot procession) with jatar hosting days
fairs.when: Booking announced around Ashwin Sankranti (mid-Sept); the yatra itself starts late October/November
fairs.what_happens: Devotee families reserve days in advance at Bakhari Kothi to host the deity's rath as it tours villages along a set route.

rituals_customs: Devotee families reserve a 'jatar' day at Bakhari Kothi to host the deity's rath during its touring yatra.
Gold is avoided as an offering since Mahunag's murti (idol) is silver.
On the last Monday of Shravan, devotees hold puja, bhajan-kirtan and small bhandaras at the temple.
visiting: The main temple is at Bakhari Kothi, roughly 25 km from Karsog town.
A separate, smaller Mahunag shrine also exists at Naldehra near Shimla, built in the same tradition — a different, related temple, not the main Karsog shrine.

mamleshwar.place: Mamel village, Karsog, Mandi district, Himachal Pradesh
mamleshwar.summary: Mamleshwar Mahadev is an ancient wood-and-stone Shiva temple in Mamel village near Karsog, regarded locally as one of the valley's oldest shrines. Tradition links it to the Pandavas' exile, and it preserves relics said to date from that period: an ever-burning sacred fire, a giant fossilised wheat grain, and a wooden drum attributed to Bhima. It also presides as senior deity over Karsog's main annual fair, the Nalwar Mela.
legend: Locals believe the temple dates back roughly 5,000 years, spanning the Satya, Treta and Dwapara (Mahabharata) ages.
Tradition holds the Pandavas stayed in Mamel during their exile (agyatvas) and Bhima killed a man-eating demon terrorising the village, an event some connect to the origin of the name 'Karsog'.
The ever-burning sacred fire (akhand dhuni) is said to have been lit by Bhima to mark his victory over the demon, burning continuously since.
A large fossil-like wheat grain (roughly 150-250 grams by various accounts) is believed to be one grown by the Pandavas here, at a spot now marked by the Annapurna Mata (Kharasna/Tara Devi) temple.
A wooden drum over 6 feet long, said to be made from bhekhal wood, is attributed to Bhima.
Tradition credits Parshuram with installing the Shiva-Parvati idol; the murti is an eight-metal (ashtadhatu) idol, said to be rare for a Shiva temple.
A separate legend traces the name 'Mamleshwar' to sage Bhrigu, who married a kinnar maiden named Mamlesha and, to atone, installed and worshipped Shiva here, giving the deity and village their names.
The temple is a protected historic pahari-pagoda-style wood-and-stone structure with a slate roof, on a raised platform.

fairs.name: Nalwar Mela, Karsog (district-level fair)
fairs.when: Usually early-to-mid April, but depends yearly on official/High Court permission for the ground; sometimes reduced to a smaller trade fair
fairs.what_happens: Opens with a shobha yatra of Mamleshwar Mahadev, sometimes joined by other valley deities (Maa Kamaksha, and in 2026 for the first time Nag Chawasi Siddh); includes women's folk-dance (naati), cultural nights.

fairs.name: Lahaul Mela (Shiv-Parvati wedding celebration)
fairs.when: Fixed date, 18 April each year
fairs.what_happens: Marks the symbolic wedding of Shiva and Parvati; Mamleshwar Mahadev travels together with Maa Kamaksha, with bhajan and puja held at the fair.

fairs.name: Shravan (monsoon month) Monday observance and Kanwar Yatra
fairs.when: Every Monday in Shravan (roughly July-August); a Kanwar Yatra to Haridwar sets off around the same time
fairs.what_happens: Devotees offer milk and water (doodh-jal) to the Shiva lingam; kanwariyas from the area also depart for Haridwar, sent off with blessings from the temple's panchayat.

rituals_customs: Devotees offer milk and water (doodh-jal) to the Shiva lingam on the last Shravan Monday.
The temple keeps an akhand dhuni (perpetually burning fire) regarded with deep reverence.
The Bhima drum and wheat grain are kept on display for darshan by pilgrims.
At district fairs, Sameshwar Mahadev traditionally dances and sits to Mamleshwar's left, a long-established seating protocol.
visiting: The temple is in Mamel village, close to Karsog town, roughly 100 km from Shimla.
Architecture is traditional Himachali wood-and-stone pahari style, with a slate roof, recognised/protected as historic.

narsingh.place: Purana Bazaar, Karsog (idol within the Laxmi Narayan temple complex)
narsingh.summary: Narsingh Bhagwan is worshipped as part of the Laxmi Narayan temple complex in Karsog's Purana Bazaar, with a daily evening aarti. The deity also has an annual jayanti (birth anniversary) procession in which Karsog's Mool Mahunag participates.

fairs.name: Shri Narsingh Dev Jayanti procession
fairs.when: Around mid-to-late May
fairs.what_happens: Brahmins perform puja for the town and world's welfare; Shri Mool Mahunag (Shirgal) departs for the temple in the evening (kalsham) and devotees are asked to gather at the temple courtyard in the early afternoon before the rath yatra.

rituals_customs: A daily evening aarti for Narsingh Bhagwan is held at the Laxmi Narayan temple, Purana Bazaar, and is sometimes shared live.
visiting: Idol is part of the Laxmi Narayan temple complex, Purana Bazaar, Karsog.

pali_nag.summary: Pali Nag is a village deity at Kali, Karsog, whose story is kept alive locally through folk performance rather than large public fairs in the material seen so far.
legend: Local folk artists perform a traditional piece about 'Pali Nag Maharaj' and the sacred confluence (sangam) of Imla and Bimla, suggesting a local legend around these paired sacred sites/streams, though the full story was not described in the post itself.
rituals_customs: A senior folk artist from Panjrat village is noted for performing this Pali Nag Maharaj/Imla-Bimla piece as part of a decades-long repertoire of local Karsog folk theatre and Karyala performances.
visiting: Village seat at Kali, Karsog.

pangna.summary: Mahamaya Devi's temple at Pangna is one of the oldest wooden temples in the Karsog area, said to have been built roughly 820 years ago by a Suket king. It stands in the traditional 'kashtkuni' (timber-bonded stone) style, valued locally for its earthquake resistance. The nearby Gihn Nag temple at Sarahi is also part of the wider Pangna deity landscape.
legend: Locals believe the temple was founded after a king's daughter was buried alive for six months to prove her purity, and emerged unharmed; the temple was built to mark this event.
Locals say Sarahi village, near the Gihn Nag temple, was once the capital of a historic princely area referred to as 'Kushraj'.

fairs.name: Katal Mela (Shri Gihn Nag), Pangna
fairs.when: Early June, around 8-11 June
fairs.what_happens: A multi-day village fair at Katal with cultural evenings and stalls.

rituals_customs: The Mahamaya temple's wooden kashtkuni construction (stacked stone-and-timber courses pinned with large wooden pegs) is locally described as earthquake-resistant.
A full Devi Bhagwat Katha at the Mahamaya temple is a rare event, last held roughly 20-25 years before a September 2026 report that preparations for a new one were underway.
The Gihn Nag temple at Sarahi, built in the traditional 'kothi' style with carved doors and window screens, had a pedhi-aur-chhatar (chariot-canopy) pratishtha ceremony in 2025.
visiting: Pangna is a sub-tehsil area of Karsog subdivision; the Mahamaya temple and the Gihn Nag temple at nearby Sarahi are both local landmarks.

pundri.place: Kao, near Karsog (shares the Maa Kamaksha temple precinct)
pundri.summary: Nag Pundri travels closely alongside Maa Kamaksha of Kao on nearly all her major journeys, and is also one of the three deities honoured at the annual Kunho Mela along with Nag Dhamuni.

fairs.name: Kunho (Kunnu) Mela
fairs.when: 3-day fair, usually 7-9 August
fairs.what_happens: Maa Kamaksha, Nag Pundri and Nag Dhamuni Kunho are welcomed with a shobha yatra and floral welcome by area women's groups.

fairs.name: Barshail Mela, Lalag
fairs.when: Fixed dates, 2-3 June
fairs.what_happens: Maa Kamaksha and Nag Pundri travel together by chariot to this fair.

rituals_customs: Nag Pundri also attended the state-level Suket Devta Mela at Sundernagar alongside Maa Kamaksha in 2025.
visiting: Shares the Maa Kamaksha temple precinct at Kao, near Karsog.

shikari_devi.place: Shikari peak, near Janjehli, Karsog area, Mandi district, Himachal Pradesh
shikari_devi.summary: Shikari Devi temple sits at roughly 3,300-3,360 metres (about 11,000 feet) on the highest peak in Mandi district, making it one of the highest temples in the region and earning it the nickname 'Crown of Mandi'. Its most famous feature is that the shrine has no roof, and locals believe that despite heavy snowfall the idol itself never gathers snow. Tradition connects the site to the Pandavas' exile and to the sage Markandeya's penance.
legend: Locals believe the temple was established by the Pandavas during their period of exile (agyatvas), when they are said to have worshipped the goddess here in the form of a deer that appeared before them.
Tradition holds that sage Markandeya performed years of tapasya (penance) at this spot, and that Goddess Durga, pleased by his devotion, manifested here in her shakti form.
Locals believe that despite heavy snow all around the temple, snow never settles on the main idol or, in some accounts, within the temple courtyard itself.
According to local tradition, many attempts over the years to build a roof over the shrine have failed, and this is regarded as the goddess's own wish or a divine mystery.

The name 'Shikari Devi' (hunter's goddess) is explained by tradition as coming from hunters (shikaris) who, in earlier times, worshipped the goddess here for success in the hunt before venturing into the surrounding dense forest.
Some posts describe the temple as home to 64 yoginis, and mention that Shikari Mata is therefore also referred to as 'Jogini Mata'.

Locals say that a devotee only reaches this remote temple when the goddess herself extends an unspoken 'call' (bulava); an unexplained strong urge to visit, or unusually smooth travel arrangements, are read as signs of this call.

fairs.name: Navratri gathering at Shikari Devi
fairs.when: During Navratri (spring and autumn, per the Hindu lunar calendar)
fairs.what_happens: Increased footfall for special puja during Navratri; posts describe devotional gatherings rather than one large organised fair.

rituals_customs: Devotees make the difficult trek or drive-plus-climb (including around 500 steps at the end of the road journey) to reach the temple, considered part of the pilgrimage's significance.
A regular bus service connects Sundernagar to Shikari Devi via Chailchowk, Bagsyad, Thunag and Janjehli, used by pilgrims and tourists especially in season.
The temple and surrounding area falls within a designated wildlife sanctuary where hunting is prohibited, a detail some posts note in connection with the 'hunter's goddess' legend.
The temple closes to visitors in winter due to heavy snowfall and road blockages, and administrative advisories are sometimes issued warning devotees not to attempt the journey during snowfall.
visiting: Elevation is consistently given in the roughly 2,850-3,360 metre (about 9,350-11,000 feet) range across posts, at the highest peak in Mandi district.
Access routes mentioned are via Janjehli, Bagsaid/Bagsyad, Kandha, or from the Karsog valley side; the final stretch to the temple is a trek through dense deodar and pine forest.
Best visiting times noted are April to June and September to November; the temple is generally not accessible in winter due to snow.
A direct bus service runs from Sundernagar via Janjehli during the travel season, with fares and a rough schedule mentioned in posts (departs Sundernagar early morning, arrives late morning).

shiv_gufa.summary: The Shiv Gufa at Saraur, near Tattapani, is an ancient natural cave shrine that was partly submerged by the Kol Dam reservoir on the Sutlej, making it hard to reach. It draws worshippers especially around Mahashivratri.

fairs.name: Mahashivratri jagran / Shiv katha at Tattapani
fairs.when: Around Mahashivratri (Feb-March, Phalgun Krishna Chaturdashi)
fairs.what_happens: A Shiv-katha and jagran (all-night vigil) held at Tattapani around Mahashivratri, connected to devotion at the Shiv Gufa.

rituals_customs: The cave was submerged by the Kol Dam hydroelectric project on the Sutlej; a local visitor reported reaching it again in December 2025 after roughly 10 years, and documented its condition at the time.
visiting: Located at Saraur, near Tattapani; access has been difficult since the Kol Dam reservoir formed, and the site is now mostly reached only when water levels allow.

suket_devta_mela.place: Sundernagar, Mandi district (deities travel there from Karsog and other former Suket-state areas)
suket_devta_mela.summary: The Suket Devta Mela is a state-level fair held at Sundernagar where local deities (devtas) from across the old Suket princely state, including many from the Karsog valley, gather in chariots. It is organised each year by the Suket Sarv Devta Committee, and locals say it was formally started by the Suket kings in 1902 in honour of Mool Mahunag ji of Bakhari Kothi, Karsog. Deities and their attendants (devlus) travel on foot over many days to reach the mela, with the chief deity of Karsog, Mool Mahunag ji, walking about 120 km every year without fail.
legend: Locals believe the mela was instituted by the Suket rulers to honour Mool Mahunag ji (worshipped as an incarnation of Raja Karna from the Mahabharata) after the deity helped a Suket king father a son and later freed him from captivity; in gratitude the king dedicated half his rule to the deity.
According to tradition, the fair has run since 1902 and Mool Mahunag ji has walked from Bakhari Kothi (Karsog) to Sundernagar every year since.
Old (1940s-era) film footage is said to show Karsog deities attending the mela even then, which locals cite as proof of how old the custom is.
In 2026 locals described the arrival of Garhpati Nag Chawasi Siddh ji of Mahog (Chawasi area, Karsog) as historic, saying the deity had not attended for about 170-180 years.

fairs.name: Suket Devta Mela
fairs.when: State-level fair at Sundernagar, usually in March-April; exact dates are fixed each year by the Suket Sarv Devta Committee and vary
fairs.what_happens: Each deity leaves its home temple in a decorated chariot (rath) with musicians (banjantari) playing traditional instruments, walking for several days with overnight halts (e.g. Karsog's Purana Bazaar) before reaching Sundernagar. A grand opening procession (shahi jaleb) is held, deities are seated at allotted spots on the mela ground, and there are cultural evenings, a rath/chariot-decoration competition, and a formal closing after which deities head home. In 2024 organisers said 165 deities took part across the whole mela.

rituals_customs: Deities travel in decorated chariots (rath) with a ceremonial umbrella/canopy (chhatra) and are accompanied by devlus (attendants) and banjantari (traditional musicians with drums and shehnai/gujju).
A deity's departure and arrival dates are announced in advance so devotees along the route can gather to receive its blessing.

The Suket Sarv Devta Committee sets rules for participation (e.g. a deity must be brought with proper instruments and formal party) and organises seating arrangements for the deities on the mela ground.
visiting: The mela takes place at Sundernagar town in Mandi district, not in Karsog itself; Karsog's own deities travel there and back over several days on foot.

sunani_kot.name_en: Shri Nag Sunani & Shri Kot Nag
sunani_kot.name_hi: श्री नाग सुनानी व श्री कोट नाग
sunani_kot.summary: Nag Sunani and Dev Thala are honoured together each year at a fair in Banglaadhar, Churag, marking the ceremonial meeting (milan) of the two deities.

fairs.name: Nag Sunani & Dev Thala Mela, Banglaadhar (Churag)
fairs.name_hi: श्री नाग सुनानी व देव थला मेला
fairs.when: Set by the Hindu calendar, on 29 Shravan
fairs.what_happens: A rath yatra (chariot procession) bringing the two deities together at Banglaadhar; organisers note there is no parking at the fairground and ask devotees to use public transport where possible.

visiting: Fairground at Banglaadhar, in Churag panchayat, Karsog subdivision.

tundli.summary: Nag Tundli is the presiding deity of Tundal village in Nanj, honoured each November with a two-day village fair that had lapsed for two decades before being revived in 2022.

fairs.name: Nag Tundli Mela, Nanj
fairs.when: Fixed dates, 15-16 November
fairs.what_happens: Opens on the evening of 15 November with the deity's ritual dance (dev nritya) to devotional drumming, followed by cultural-evening performances by local and guest folk singers; a two-day event.

rituals_customs: The fair's opening evening centres on the deity's own dev nritya (ritual dance), performed to devotional drumbeats before the wider cultural programme.
visiting: Temple/village seat at Tundal, in the Nanj area of Karsog.
